name: EGD with Dilation
overview: Upper endoscopy with pneumatic or bougie dilation of strictures

pimpingQuestions.question: Esophageal atresia occurs in 1:3000 births. What is the most common type and its embryologic basis?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Type C (85%): proximal atresia with distal TEF. Failure of the tracheoesophageal septum to completely separate foregut into trachea and esophagus during weeks 4-5. Associated with VACTERL in 25%.

pimpingQuestions.question: What are the three types of esophageal strictures and the appropriate dilator for each?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Simple/short (peptic, Schatzki ring): TTS balloon. Complex/long (caustic, radiation, anastomotic): Savary bougie for tactile feedback. Malignant: stenting preferred. Rule of 3: don't exceed 3 consecutive French sizes per session.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the blood supply to the esophagus at different levels?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Cervical: inferior thyroid artery. Thoracic: direct aortic branches and bronchial arteries. Abdominal: left gastric and left inferior phrenic. Thoracic perforation is most dangerous — no serosa, segmental blood supply, rapid mediastinitis.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the perforation rate of esophageal dilation?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Bougie: 0.1-0.4%. Balloon: 0.1-0.3%. Malignant strictures: up to 10%. Signs: chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, Hamman's sign. CT with oral water-soluble contrast is diagnostic.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is a Schatzki ring, and at what diameter does it cause dysphagia?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Thin mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction (GEJ), containing only mucosa and submucosa. Dysphagia at <13mm. Treatment: single dilation to >16mm. Always biopsy for eosinophilic esophagitis (10-15% of food impactions).
